title: The One Where Rachels Sister Babysits

jokes.text: Ross confesses he's also never given Emma frosting from a can, implying he has in fact done exactly that
jokes.setup: Rachel and Ross are establishing that neither of them has given Emma a cookie. Ross volunteers an oddly specific denial.
jokes.punchline: "For the record, I've also never given her frosting from a can" — the specificity of the denial reveals the guilt.
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom guilt-reveal structure. The unprompted specificity of 'frosting from a can' is the tell. Works because it's character-specific to overindulgent Ross and efficiently constructed with no wasted words.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I have never given Emma a cookie!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Not even one?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No! And I certainly never used canned frosting to write her name on a cupcake!

jokes.text: "It's just that we don't think of you as really being so much with the words."
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler ask Rachel to write their adoption recommendation letter, then admit they almost didn't ask Joey.
jokes.punchline: Monica's diplomatic but devastating assessment that Joey is 'not so much with the words' — a spectacular understatement.
jokes.explanation: Monica's phrasing is characteristically passive-aggressive and roundabout. The convoluted construction 'not so much with the words' is funnier than a blunt insult would be. Good character integration for both Monica's diplomacy and Joey's known dimness.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, we were going to ask Joey, but we figured that someone who can't string together a coherent sentence probably shouldn't be writing a recommendation letter.

jokes.text: Emma babbles immediately after, as if proving Monica's point about Joey's verbal skills
jokes.setup: Monica has just said Joey isn't 'so much with the words'.
jokes.punchline: Emma the baby immediately babbles, implying even the infant communicates better — or that Joey is at the same level.
jokes.explanation: Monica's line sets it up, the baby's babble is the visual/audio punchline. Chandler's 'Clearly, we were wrong' sells it. The juxtaposition of the baby validating Monica's point about Joey is efficiently funny. Rewatch bonus for catching the timing.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I am too good with words! I know lots of words. I can use them... good. And I do it... real good.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Case in point.

jokes.text: "Dear Baby Adoption Decider People..."
jokes.setup: Joey has volunteered to write the recommendation letter and said he has 'a lot of nice stuff to say.'
jokes.punchline: His opening salutation reveals he has absolutely no idea how formal letters work.
jokes.explanation: Genuinely excellent joke. The specificity of 'Baby Adoption Decider People' is perfectly calibrated — it sounds exactly like how Joey would sincerely address such a letter. It's not random absurdism; it's authentic character logic executed with perfect economy. Highly quotable and a fan-favorite moment from this episode.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Dear To Whom It May Concern, yo, what's up?

jokes.text: Cut to Monica and Chandler's reaction shot — Monica: 'So excited about your letter'
jokes.setup: Joey has just read his opening line 'Dear Baby Adoption Decider People.'
jokes.punchline: Monica's flat, terrified 'So excited about your letter' — she is clearly the opposite of excited.
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom reaction beat. Monica's controlled panic is perfectly in character. The irony lands cleanly but isn't particularly inventive — it's a functional straight-man response to a great punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm dressing up for my anniversary no matter where we go. If Frank wants to take me to a public restroom, I'm wearing my fancy dress.

jokes.text: Phoebe answers 'Yeah' when asked what her one-year anniversary is of — first date, first kiss, or first time having sex
jokes.setup: Rachel asks which milestone Phoebe's anniversary commemorates.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's 'Yeah' implies all three happened on the same day — a gloriously economical overshare.
jokes.explanation: Economically perfect — one word does the work of several sentences. It's also very Phoebe: she's not being crude, she's being matter-of-fact. The character integration elevates what could be a cheap joke.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: He won't even use our bathroom.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I have a very delicate digestive system.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: And I'm not comfortable with the acoustic properties of that bathroom.

jokes.text: "And we're gonna have sex in a public restroom."
jokes.setup: Phoebe describes her anniversary plans — fancy clothes, fine jewelry — building toward a romantic occasion.
jokes.punchline: The list culminates with public restroom sex, presented as equally natural and exciting.
jokes.explanation: Good escalation joke — the list builds romantic expectations and then swerves hard. Phoebe's total sincerity is what makes it land rather than feel gratuitous. Works within her character's free-spirited philosophy.

jokes.text: "Chandler won't even have sex in our bathroom. That's where people make number two."
jokes.setup: Phoebe mentions public restroom sex. Monica expresses surprise that people do that.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's reasoning: the bathroom is where people 'make number two' — a bizarrely prudish and childish logic from an otherwise sarcastic adult.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the juxtaposition: Chandler is a sophisticated sarcastic adult using the childish phrase 'make number two.' This incongruity is the laugh. Also reveals a funny quirk of their marriage. Good character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Wow, what a keen observation. I had no idea I wasn't Rachel. Thank you for pointing that out.

jokes.text: Ross gives a B to a Pottery Barn catalog
jokes.setup: Ross is grading papers, distracted from Charlie's advances. She points out he gave a B to a Pottery Barn catalog.
jokes.punchline: "Well, it had some good ideas." — Ross defends the grade earnestly.
jokes.explanation: Excellent character joke. Ross is so consumed by his professorial mindset that he grades a catalog — and then DEFENDS the grade. This is perfectly in character for his obsessive academic identity. The earnestness of 'it had some good ideas' is the kicker. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Amy, it's me, Ross! We met in 1994 at Central Perk. You were sitting in that orange couch when I first saw you!

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, do I know you?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yes! We went to Barbados together! You wore that blue dress! We danced all night!

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.line: I think you have me confused with someone else, sir.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, Amy, listen - I'm a paleontologist! Remember? You used to make fun of my dinosaur jokes at Thanksgiving!

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.line: Are you selling something? Because I'm not interested in whatever this is.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm not selling anything! I'm your... we spent ten years together! TEN YEARS!

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.line: Well, that'll be five dollars for the hot dog, thanks.

jokes.text: "You're not Rachel." / "Still sharp as a tack."
jokes.setup: Amy barges in asking for Rachel; Ross opens the door. Amy states the obvious.
jokes.punchline: Ross's 'Still sharp as a tack' — a withering sarcastic response establishing Amy's dim nature immediately.
jokes.explanation: A reliable but not especially inventive sarcastic comeback. It efficiently establishes the Amy/Ross dynamic and Amy's obliviousness. The phrase itself is a common expression, but it's deployed well here.

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.line: Did you sell my falafel?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, I didn't sell your falafel.

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.line: Well, it's gone!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I know, but I didn't sell it.

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.line: Then where is it?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Fine. Yes. I sold your falafel. I'm a falafel scalper. I buy them up, sell them on the street corner. It's a very lucrative business.

jokes.text: Amy fails to recognize Ross despite his escalating reminders of their shared history
jokes.setup: Ross tries to remind Amy who he is: grew up on her block, had Thanksgiving together, had a baby with her sister.
jokes.punchline: Amy: 'Did I buy a falafel from you yesterday?' — she finally 'recognizes' him as a street vendor, not Rachel's long-term partner.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest jokes. The escalating list of intimacies (block, Thanksgiving, fathered her niece) builds comic pressure, and the falafel punchline is brilliantly unexpected and specific. It's funny on multiple levels: Amy's shocking self-absorption, the callback to the earlier Ross/falafel exchange being planted for this payoff, and Ross's humiliation. The structure is textbook misdirection done right.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You recognized me! From Days of Our Lives?

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.line: Yeah, I watched it. Your acting was terrible.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? Terrible?

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.line: Awful. Really bad. You were the worst part of that show.

jokes.text: Ross confirms: "Yes. Yes, you did." — accepting the falafel vendor identity
jokes.setup: Amy has just asked if she bought a falafel from Ross yesterday, as if that's the only context in which she knows him.
jokes.punchline: Ross, defeated, simply confirms it — giving up on correcting her.
jokes.explanation: The defeated acceptance is funnier than any protestation would be. Ross's willingness to just go along with it milks the joke perfectly. The 'Yes. Yes, you did.' rhythm — with the pause — is a great beat.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh, so now I'm just some guy who can't remember his daughter's name? What's next, I'm going to forget where I work? 'Oh, I'm Ross, I sell... I don't know, falafel?'

jokes.text: "Always nice to meet a fan."
jokes.setup: Amy has just told Joey he 'is not good' as an actor.
jokes.punchline: Joey pretends to take it as fandom, either missing the insult or brilliantly deflecting it.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly in Joey's character — his ego is so intact that criticism slides off him. The ambiguity of whether he's being sarcastic or genuine makes it funnier. His unshakeable confidence is a reliable comedic engine.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yes, hello, welcome to my falafel stand. What can I get for you today?

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.line: Wow, your English is really improving! You know, for someone from... over there. You're very articulate for a falafel guy.

jokes.text: "What do I know? I just sell Middle Eastern food from a cart." / "Hey, your English is getting better."
jokes.setup: Amy has just 'recognized' Ross as the falafel vendor. He leans into the bit sarcastically.
jokes.punchline: Amy's 'Your English is getting better' — she is completely sold on the fiction that Ross is an immigrant street vendor.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback execution. Ross commits to the bit sarcastically, but Amy takes it completely literally and compliments his 'improving English.' The joke rewards the setup from earlier and deepens Amy's characterization as breathtakingly oblivious. The layers here — Ross's sarcasm, Amy's sincerity, the racial/class assumptions embedded in Amy's response — are well-crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I hate her. She's so annoying and self-centered and... and I love her.

jokes.text: "She may be the hottest girl I've ever hated."
jokes.setup: Joey has observed Amy's rudeness and beauty simultaneously.
jokes.punchline: His verdict: she's the hottest girl he's ever hated — a confession that reveals his conflicted priorities.
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable lines in the episode. The construction is perfect: it validates his hatred while simultaneously undermining it with his attraction. Pure Joey philosophy in one sentence. High quotability and excellent character integration — this could only be Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey, why don't you use a thesaurus?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I don't know what that means.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: It's a book of synonyms.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh, I don't need a thesaurus. I know lots of big words.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey, you just said you didn't know what a thesaurus was.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, what is a thesaurus?

jokes.text: "My God, that's great. I'm smart. No, no, I'm: 'Brainy, bright, clever.' I love this thing!"
jokes.setup: Joey discovers the thesaurus function and finds synonyms for 'smart.'
jokes.punchline: He immediately corrects himself using thesaurus words to describe himself — with zero self-awareness that the tool is for the letter, not for him.
jokes.explanation: Joey immediately redirects the tool toward self-admiration. The thesaurus has become a vanity mirror. This is authentic Joey logic — technology exists to serve Joey's ego first. Solid character-driven escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, check it out! I got this thesaurus and it's making me smarter!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Check out this word... 'play.' You can also say 'frolic,' 'cavort,' or... 'bone.'

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: From now on, I'm gonna bone all night long!

jokes.text: "He has a killer apartment." / "And it's on Fifth." / "And the elevator opens up right into the living room."
jokes.setup: Amy announces she's getting married. The group asks what the guy is like.
jokes.punchline: Amy describes the apartment exclusively, with no reference to the man's personality until pressured.
jokes.explanation: Good escalating character comedy. Each answer about the apartment rather than the man deepens the joke. The rhythm of withholding a human quality about the fiancé while lavishing detail on real estate is very funny and entirely consistent with Amy's shallow priorities.

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.line: So beautiful.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Thank you! She really is precious, isn't she?

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.line: What? Oh, no, I'm talking about your sheets. What thread count is this?

jokes.text: "But he travels a lot, so he's hardly ever there."
jokes.setup: Amy has described her fiancé as 'old.' The group is processing the age gap.
jokes.punchline: Amy adds that the best feature of the man she's marrying is that he's rarely home.
jokes.explanation: Another efficient character reveal — Amy frames her fiancé's absence as a positive feature. This is consistent, specific to Amy, and delivered with her characteristic obliviousness. Good but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: So what's your fiancé like?

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.line: Oh, he's wonderful! He has this amazing apartment in the city with hardwood floors, stainless steel appliances, and a walk-in closet. The master bedroom has an en-suite bathroom with heated towel racks, and there's a balcony with a view of the park.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No, I mean what's he like as a person?

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.line: Oh! Well, the kitchen has granite countertops and a Sub-Zero refrigerator. Plus it's rent-controlled!

jokes.text: "God, we used to make out all the time after you went to sleep."
jokes.setup: Rachel uses Barry (her ex-fiancé) as an example of someone she didn't love but almost married. Amy says 'Remember him?'
jokes.punchline: Amy admits she and Barry used to make out behind Rachel's back — presented as fond nostalgia rather than a confession.
jokes.explanation: Genuinely excellent joke. The reveal is shocking but completely in character for Amy. The delivery — casual, even wistful — is perfect. It retroactively makes Rachel's past worse while simultaneously being a funny character revelation. Amy's total lack of shame or even awareness that this is a confession is the comedic engine. The 'after you went to sleep' detail is a brilliant specific touch.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait, you're marrying Mark's father?

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, he's really successful and—

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Amy! That's Mark's dad!

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.line: I know! It's actually perfect. I get to see Mark at all the family dinners, and it'll be so awkward for him.

jokes.text: "Sometimes just nodding is okay."
jokes.setup: Amy has just casually confessed to making out with Rachel's ex-fiancé. Rachel needs to redirect the conversation.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's weary advice to Amy that silence would have been fine — an underreaction that acknowledges the horror without dwelling on it.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — five words to encapsulate a perfectly calibrated reaction. Rachel doesn't explode (which would be predictable) but instead offers calm life advice. The underreaction is funnier than the alternative.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Barry was such a jerk.

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.line: Oh, about that... I may have hooked up with him a few times while you guys were together.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: WHAT?!

jokes.text: "You're right. I'm gonna marry Myron and keep looking for Mr. Right."
jokes.setup: Rachel gives Amy a heartfelt speech about deserving true love and not marrying someone she doesn't love.
jokes.punchline: Amy takes the speech as permission to have both — marry for the apartment AND continue searching for real love.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant subversion of a sincere moment. Rachel's heartfelt advice completely misfires because Amy processes it through her own self-serving logic. The audience is set up for a touching breakthrough, then Amy perfectly demolishes it. Very well-structured.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Okay, Amy, I'm gonna need you to stop talking now.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Like, immediately.

jokes.text: Phoebe argues with a stranger about nachos blocking her seat at the Knicks game, saying 'It's my anniversary'
jokes.setup: Phoebe arrives at the basketball game in formal attire for her anniversary.
jokes.punchline: She is in a mundane dispute about nachos obscuring her seat, treating 'it's my anniversary' as a trump card in nacho negotiations.
jokes.explanation: Mildly amusing visual setup — overdressed woman asserting anniversary privilege over nachos. The joke is mostly in the visual incongruity of Phoebe's formal wear at a basketball game. Not particularly deep, but functional.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You shouldn't settle. You need to find someone you really love, someone who makes you happy.

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.line: You're right, you're absolutely right. I'm going to marry for money and cheat on him.

jokes.text: Phoebe and Mike shout their love declarations, escalating in volume, to each other in the arena
jokes.setup: Phoebe and Mike are sharing a romantic moment about their anniversary at the basketball game.
jokes.punchline: Their declarations escalate in volume and intensity until they're shouting in a crowded arena, with the final declaration — 'You're amazing in bed!' — bellowed publicly.
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom escalation. The joke is predictable in structure but executed with enough energy to work. The public overshare of 'amazing in bed' is the peak. Functional comedy but not particularly inventive.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Excuse me, could you move your nachos? That's my seat.

dialogue.speaker: Fan
dialogue.line: Oh, sorry about that.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Thank you. And while you're at it, I'm going to need a better seat. It's my anniversary.

dialogue.speaker: Fan
dialogue.line: Your anniversary of what?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Of my birth! I was born!

jokes.text: "How lame. It's so tacky and impersonal." — Phoebe watches a Jumbotron proposal, unaware Mike planned the same
jokes.setup: An on-screen proposal appears on the Jumbotron. Phoebe immediately critiques it.
jokes.punchline: The audience knows (and will soon confirm) that Mike had planned exactly this for Phoebe — making her critique an ironic self-own.
jokes.explanation: Good dramatic irony setup. The audience is ahead of Phoebe, which creates the tension that sustains the entire Phoebe/Mike storyline. The payoff is well-planted here. Rewatch bonus because knowing the setup makes this funnier retroactively.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: It's our anniversary!

dialogue.speaker: Stranger
dialogue.line: ...And?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: And what? We're in love!

jokes.text: "It's the longest I ever spent on a computer without looking at porn."
jokes.setup: Joey presents the finished recommendation letter to Monica and Chandler, proud of his effort.
jokes.punchline: His measure of hard work is how long he went without looking at porn.
jokes.explanation: Joey brags about computer discipline using an entirely Joey-specific metric. The joke is about what he considers a sacrifice versus what a normal person would consider a sacrifice. Good character integration and highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, that's so unoriginal! A big screen proposal? Everyone does that. When Mike proposes to me, it's gonna be something special, something nobody's ever seen before.

jokes.text: "They are humid, prepossessing Homo sapiens with full-sized aortic pumps."
jokes.setup: Chandler asks Joey what the original sentence was before he used the thesaurus on every word.
jokes.punchline: The thesaurized version: 'They are humid, prepossessing Homo sapiens with full-sized aortic pumps' — a clinically absurd translation of 'warm, nice people with big hearts.'
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode and a strong contender for the best in this episode. The word-by-word thesaurus substitution is a brilliant comedic premise, and 'humid, prepossessing Homo sapiens with full-sized aortic pumps' is perfectly constructed absurdist comedy. Each substitution is individually hilarious ('warm→humid', 'big hearts→full-sized aortic pumps') and the cumulative effect is magnificent. The payoff fully justifies the buildup. Highly quotable, would become a fan-favorite moment.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, so I'm writing this recommendation letter, right? And I'm telling them all about my computer skills.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm like, 'I use the computer every single day. Sometimes for hours.'

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Mostly just... you know, looking at stuff. Sometimes I look at the same stuff twice.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh! And I know how to turn it off. Well, I know how to make it go to sleep. I don't actually know how to turn it off.

jokes.text: "Well, because you signed it: 'Baby Kangaroo Tribbiani.'"
jokes.setup: Chandler tells Joey they can't use the letter. Joey asks why.
jokes.punchline: Joey signed the letter 'Baby Kangaroo Tribbiani' — a reference to his thesaurus substitution of 'joey' (a baby kangaroo).
jokes.explanation: This may be the single best joke in the episode. The logic is airtight: Joey used the thesaurus on every word, looked up 'Joey,' found 'baby kangaroo,' and signed his own name incorrectly. The fact that this is implied rather than explained makes the audience do a beat of work and feel rewarded. The name 'Baby Kangaroo Tribbiani' is objectively hilarious as a string of words. This is the kind of joke that gets quoted for decades. It earns every craft point.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm gonna go get some coffee.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm gonna perambulate and ingest a caffeinated beverage.

jokes.text: "Just write from here. Your full-sized aortic pump."
jokes.setup: Chandler tells Joey to stop trying to sound smart and write from the heart.
jokes.punchline: He corrects himself using Joey's thesaurus language: 'your full-sized aortic pump.'
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback. Chandler adopts the thesaurus language mid-sincere-advice, which is a funny character move (he can't resist the joke even in a teachable moment) and rewards the audience for remembering the earlier punchline. Well-integrated.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Baby Kangaroo? That's what he signs his letters with?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: It's my nickname!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Baby Kangaroo Tribbiani?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, my agent started calling me that.

jokes.text: "I am Erin Brockovich."
jokes.setup: Amy announces she took Rachel's advice and left Myron. Rachel praises her.
jokes.punchline: Amy declares herself Erin Brockovich — a woman who famously fought a corporation for justice — for dumping a man she barely liked to get his apartment.
jokes.explanation: Good character joke — Amy's grandiose self-image is hilariously disproportionate to her actual act of bravery. The Erin Brockovich reference gives the joke a specific pop-culture anchor that makes it land harder.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You need to write from the heart, Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: From the heart? You mean from the... tickle-pumpy?

jokes.text: "But Erin Brockovich had her own house."
jokes.setup: Amy has compared herself to Erin Brockovich, then immediately asks if she can move in with Rachel.
jokes.punchline: Rachel punctures the metaphor: Erin Brockovich was self-sufficient; Amy is immediately asking for a place to stay.
jokes.explanation: Quick and sharp callback that immediately deflates Amy's self-mythology. The Erin Brockovich callback is used twice within seconds, which works because the second usage is the puncture of the first. Economical and effective.

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.line: I left Myron! I took your advice, Rachel.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, that's amazing! I'm so proud of you!

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.line: I know. I'm like Rosa Parks.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What?!

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.line: I sat down and I refused to move.

jokes.text: Amy kept kicking Rachel and yelling 'Myron, get off!' in her sleep
jokes.setup: Rachel slept on the couch because Amy took her bed.
jokes.punchline: Amy's sleep behavior reveals she was apparently in a physical altercation with Myron even in her subconscious.
jokes.explanation: Funny detail that also circles back to Amy's distaste for Myron even subconsciously. The specific name 'Myron' makes it funnier, as does the ambiguity of what exactly Myron was doing that required that instruction.

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.line: I'm like Erin Brockovich. I'm independent, I'm smart, and I have a really nice ass.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Okay, but Erin Brockovich had a job.

jokes.text: "'A moment on the lips, forever on the hips.' I don't need that kind of talk in my house!"
jokes.setup: Joey is trying to get Rachel to kick Amy out. He recounts Amy's crime: criticizing his pizza eating.
jokes.punchline: Joey's outrage that someone would question his eating habits in his own home — the pizza-shaming is a genuine grievance to him.
jokes.explanation: Funny because Joey treats food criticism with the seriousness of a profound personal violation. His home is a food-judgment-free zone in his mind. The character specificity is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: She said I eat too much and I'm getting fat!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Me? Getting fat? I'm Joey Tribbiani!

jokes.text: "Because we'll appreciate it more when she's gone?"
jokes.setup: Rachel says keeping Amy around is 'really good' and that something positive will come of it.
jokes.punchline: Joey guesses the silver lining: they'll appreciate normal life more after Amy leaves.
jokes.explanation: Joey's hopeful negative interpretation is a solid small laugh. It's not particularly crafted but it's true to his character and delivered with the right energy.

jokes.text: "Yeah. Monica made us."
jokes.setup: Rachel says 'you guys really took care of me' when she first came to New York.
jokes.punchline: Joey confirms they helped — but clarifies it was under Monica's orders, not voluntary goodwill.
jokes.explanation: Good small character joke that gets a laugh through its blunt honesty. Monica as group enforcer is a consistent running character trait. Joey's honesty is characteristically unfiltered.

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.line: Are you sure you want to eat that?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yes, I'm sure. And you know what? I'm going to enjoy every single bite.

jokes.text: "That's what I'm wearing today. That's why I hung it on the door."
jokes.setup: Amy has taken one of Rachel's outfits from the closet and is wearing it.
jokes.punchline: Amy defends herself with logic that makes sense only to someone with zero boundaries — she announced her intention by hanging it on the door.
jokes.explanation: Amy's internal logic is consistent with her character — she created a system and expects it to be respected, regardless of whose clothes they are. Good cringe character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's right, I'm a poet and didn't even know it. Fo' shizzle.

jokes.text: "Oh, sweetie, you can't pull this off."
jokes.setup: Amy is wearing Rachel's outfit and apparently commenting on Rachel's fashion choices.
jokes.punchline: Amy, while wearing Rachel's clothes without permission, tells Rachel she can't 'pull off' her own outfit.
jokes.explanation: The irony is built in: Amy is critiquing Rachel's style while wearing Rachel's own clothing without permission. The double-layer of entitlement is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You know, the problem with you guys is that you're always trying to impress women by being all sensitive and in touch with your feelings. What you need to do is just be yourself, be confident, show them you're a real man who knows what he wants and isn't afraid to— wait, why am I the one giving this advice?

jokes.text: "I'm curvy and I like it!"
jokes.setup: Amy has implied Rachel shouldn't eat something ('Sure you want to eat that?') and Monica is nearby.
jokes.punchline: Monica pre-emptively defends her right to eat, delivering a declaration about her body image — but hilariously directed at no one in particular.
jokes.explanation: Monica's instant defensiveness about food — given her history with eating — is a classic character-specific reaction. The delivery of 'I'm curvy and I like it!' as a battle cry is funny even if the joke itself isn't deeply inventive.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You should propose to him at Foot Locker.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Foot Locker?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: He would never expect it. It's perfect.

jokes.text: "Well, I bought Chandler a $500 watch, and he wrote me a rap song."
jokes.setup: Phoebe says she had the worst anniversary ever. Monica challenges her with their worst anniversary story.
jokes.punchline: The profound gift asymmetry: a $500 watch versus a rap song Chandler wrote himself.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the specificity — a $500 watch is a real sacrifice; a rap song is Chandler's creative delusion. It also characterizes Chandler as someone who thought this was equivalent. Monica's delivery of 'Word' (imitating Chandler's rap sign-off) is a perfect button.

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.line: Nana is on the phone.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Amy, Nana's been dead for ten years.

jokes.text: "Seriously?" / "Word."
jokes.setup: Monica has just revealed Chandler wrote her a rap song as an anniversary gift.
jokes.punchline: Monica drops 'Word' as confirmation — channeling Chandler's rap persona in a single devastating syllable.
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy — one word as the entire punchline and callback combined. 'Word' is the perfect choice because it simultaneously confirms the story and embodies Chandler's ill-advised rap affectation. Excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: My throat hurts like the nanny's menstrual cramps.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I don't think that's biologically possible.

jokes.text: Phoebe asks 'Seriously?' about the rap, and Chandler replies 'Word.'
jokes.setup: Monica has just admitted Chandler gave her a rap song for their anniversary.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's response to Phoebe's incredulous 'Seriously?' is the hip-hop affirmation 'Word' — playing the bit straight while confirming the absurdity.
jokes.explanation: One of the best buttons in the episode. 'Word' is maximally economical — one word that confirms, commits to the bit, and reveals Chandler's odd pride in his rap gift. Near-perfect economy score. The juxtaposition of Chandler's buttoned-up persona with hip-hop slang is very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.line: I wasn't actually in the bathroom. I was standing right here listening to everything you said.

jokes.text: "She's right. If I were a guy and... Did I just say, 'If I were a guy'?"
jokes.setup: Monica is trying to empathize with Mike's perspective about Phoebe's proposal-ruining comments.
jokes.punchline: She catches herself starting a sentence with 'If I were a guy' — implying she's so deep in the scenario she forgot she's a married woman.
jokes.explanation: Light self-aware beat. It's a mild, competent joke that gets a small chuckle. The comic self-correction is a standard sitcom device but executed cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: How did the adoption agency know Joey was a child?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: The agency worker estimated Joey's age from his childlike artwork.

jokes.text: "Isn't that a little desperate?" / "I proposed to Chandler." / "All right, moving on."
jokes.setup: Rachel suggests Phoebe propose to Mike. Phoebe worries it seems desperate. Monica points out she proposed to Chandler.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's instant pivot — 'All right, moving on' — the fastest non-argument she's ever made.
jokes.explanation: Good two-beat joke. Monica's callback to her own proposal is a character detail. Phoebe's 'Moving on' is funny because it acknowledges Monica's point is devastating without engaging with it. Economical.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Amy! You pierced Emma's ears?! What were you thinking?!

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.line: Well, she looks absolutely adorable now. The little studs really bring out her eyes.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: That's not the point! She's a baby!

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.line: I know, and that's why I did it now. When you're young, the holes close up so easily if you change your mind. Plus, pierced ears are really elegant.

jokes.text: Monica reveals she proposed to Chandler, then the group awkwardly moves past it
jokes.setup: Phoebe worries that proposing to Mike would be desperate. Monica says she proposed to Chandler.
jokes.punchline: The group's response — 'All right, moving on' — implies there's something uncomfortable or emasculating about the memory that everyone agrees not to dwell on.
jokes.explanation: 'All right, moving on' as an awkward redirect is a good beat that plays on the show's history. The implication that there's something sensitive here (Chandler's pride?) that everyone tacitly avoids is well-played.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Ross is going to be so upset about Emma's ears.

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.line: What? Why would he care about her ears?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Because they stick out a little bit.

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.line: Oh, well, at least she didn't inherit his... you know, his street vendor nose.

jokes.text: "How about at a game on the big screen?" / "How about at a Foot Locker?"
jokes.setup: The group is brainstorming where Phoebe should propose to Mike. Rachel suggests the big screen (the method Phoebe already trashed).
jokes.punchline: Monica's alternative: a Foot Locker — deliberately lowering the bar even further, then immediately walking back with logic.
jokes.explanation: Mild joke. The Foot Locker non sequitur is funny but the reasoning Monica gives immediately after ('he'd never suspect it') actually makes it too logical and deflates the absurdity. Competent but not strong.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. Her ears are pierced?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yeah, I took her to get them pierced.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You did what?! Without asking me? She's three years old!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Ross, they're just earrings.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Just earrings? They're holes in her ears! Permanent holes!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Ross, the holes close up if you don't wear earrings.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Really? They close up? How long does that take?

jokes.text: "Nana's on the phone." / "That's interesting, since she died seven years ago."
jokes.setup: Rachel pulls out her phone in the middle of the conversation to respond to a call.
jokes.punchline: Ross points out her grandmother died seven years ago — the person calling cannot be who Rachel said.
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom interruption gag with a mildly dark punchline. The 'she died seven years ago' response is a reliable laugh, slightly elevated by Ross's matter-of-fact delivery.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, Monica's cool. I mean, she's not as cool as me, obviously. But she's cool in a... 'my aunt knows what a Blockbuster Video is' kind of way.

jokes.text: "She did? Who got her condo in Boca?"
jokes.setup: Ross reveals the grandmother died seven years ago.
jokes.punchline: Amy's concern is immediately: who inherited the Florida condo? She processes death as a real estate event.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Amy character joke. She processes death as a real estate opportunity with no hesitation. 'Condo in Boca' is a perfect specific detail — it's exactly the type of property Amy would want to know about. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: "For one thing, she keeps calling her Ella." / "Ella's a nice name." / "Fine, we'll call the next one Ella."
jokes.setup: Ross objects to Amy babysitting. His first reason is that Amy keeps calling Emma 'Ella.'
jokes.punchline: Rachel dismisses it; Ross concedes the name is nice and offers a compromise — their next child can be named Ella.
jokes.explanation: The joke pivots pleasantly — Ross arguing against Amy while inadvertently validating the name. The 'next one' beat implies Ross has already mentally filed this away as a future option. Competent small laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Babies don't care if you're slim.

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.line: Well, Amy's here now.

jokes.text: Rachel: 'Ella's a nice name.' Ross: 'Fine, we'll call the next one Ella.'
jokes.setup: Rachel defends the name Ella. Ross concedes — but as a future naming option for a hypothetical second child.
jokes.punchline: The pivot to 'the next one' — casually planning a second child mid-argument about a babysitter — is both funny and slightly alarming given their relationship status.
jokes.explanation: The casual assumption of 'the next one' is a great relationship joke between Ross and Rachel — it implies more than the conversation warrants. Rachel's silent 'Okay' response adds to the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: That's it! I'm warning you, Amy. If you ever do anything like that to Emma again, I'm going to have the Falafel Vendor ban you from every falafel cart in Manhattan!

jokes.text: "Listen, I couldn't help but overhear, because I was trying to."
jokes.setup: Amy has clearly been eavesdropping on Ross and Rachel's private conversation about whether to trust her with the baby.
jokes.punchline: She admits she was eavesdropping with a cheerful lack of shame — the honesty makes it funnier than a denial would.
jokes.explanation: Genuinely clever line. The structure 'I couldn't help but overhear, because I was trying to' inverts the standard apologetic eavesdrop disclaimer and makes it honest. Amy's total lack of embarrassment is on-brand. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: I need to go to the bathroom.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh no, you can't do that. If you hold it in, it goes back up into your brain and you get smarter.

jokes.text: "So how much does it pay?"
jokes.setup: Amy has given a speech about how much she wants to help, how wonderful Rachel has been, and how she really wants to do this.
jokes.punchline: The final question immediately after the speech reveals the mercenary motivation.
jokes.explanation: Classic deflation joke. The sincerity of the speech is completely punctured in five words. The timing and economy are excellent — Amy barely finishes sounding magnanimous before revealing the transaction.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No, no, no! You guys are all sexist! Women are just as capable as men!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: This is discrimination! We should all be treated equally!

jokes.text: "No can do, amigo." / Joey reveals he handwrote the letter
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler ask to see the second draft of the letter. Joey says he dropped it off already and can't print another.
jokes.punchline: He reveals he handwrote the letter — meaning there IS no copy, which contradicts what a printed letter would allow.
jokes.explanation: Joey's logic — feeling it was 'more personal' to handwrite it — is both sweet and disastrous. The 'No can do, amigo' is a funny deflection but the joke's main energy is in the panic it causes Monica and Chandler.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hello? Yes, this is he. Uh-huh. Really? Well, I'm very excited. No, no, I'm a very good listener. I do chores. I eat all my vegetables. Well, most of them. And I always say please and thank you.

jokes.text: Joey has handwritten the second draft letter instead of printing it, explaining 'it felt more personal'
jokes.setup: Chandler asks to read the new draft. Joey says he dropped it off at the agency already.
jokes.punchline: He handwrote it because it felt 'more personal' — which, while arguably true, means it's already in the agency's hands with no copy.
jokes.explanation: Setup for the later payoff. Joey's well-meaning incompetence — handwriting an unreviewed letter and already submitting it — is completely in character. The dread it creates in Monica and Chandler is the real payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Where did Jill gain the weight?

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.line: Well, I'd have to say her face, her ass, and her stomach.

jokes.text: "We're gonna be one of those old couples that collects orchids or has a lot of birds."
jokes.setup: Chandler and Monica spiral into panic about the letter going in their adoption file.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's vision of their childless future: orchids and birds — a very specific, very sad image.
jokes.explanation: Good Chandler absurdist spiral. 'Orchids or birds' is a funny specific image of lonely substitute-child hobbies. The 'or' construction implies these are two equally grim fates between which he cannot choose.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Jill was on the Atkins diet.

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.line: Oh my God, the carbohydrates are like hunting down their sister!

jokes.text: Chandler calls the agency, then hangs up defeated: 'We're screwed, aren't you? You know what? Just tell me on the way to the bird store.'
jokes.setup: Chandler calls the agency hoping to intercept Joey's letter. His end of the conversation doesn't sound good.
jokes.punchline: 'Just tell me on the way to the bird store' — Chandler has already accepted the worst and is planning their eccentric childless future.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback execution. Chandler doesn't even wait for Monica's reaction — he goes straight to accepting the bird store. The defeat and the callback land simultaneously, and 'bird store' as resigned shorthand for their fate is very quotable. Strong craft.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: What? No Balls? Mike, you have balls. I've seen them.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Phoebe, it's a figure of speech.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, it's a very confusing figure of speech because anatomically speaking, you're very well-equipped.

jokes.text: "They thought it was very smart of us to have a child write the letter." / "She guessed 8, 9, based on his drawings."
jokes.setup: Chandler calls the agency expecting disaster; instead gets good news.
jokes.punchline: The agency thought a child wrote the letter — and based on the drawings (Joey drew in the letter), estimated age 8 or 9.
jokes.explanation: Excellent payoff to the entire letter subplot. The agency's interpretation — that it was strategically charming to have a child write it — saves Mondler while simultaneously being devastating about Joey's intellect. 'She guessed 8, 9, based on his drawings' is the killer button. The specificity of the age estimate and the 'drawings' detail is perfect. One of the episode's best laugh moments.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You hid the ring in the cake? That's so unoriginal! Every proposal does that!

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: I thought you'd like it...

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, it's not romantic, it's just... predictable. You know what? You're a jerk!

jokes.text: "Babies are dull."
jokes.setup: Monica asks if the baby outing was fun.
jokes.punchline: Amy's verdict: babies are dull. No elaboration. No apology.
jokes.explanation: Three words, maximum economy. Amy's bald assessment of infanthood is funny precisely because it's so honest and unapologetic. The deadpan delivery of a genuinely anti-social opinion is a great Amy beat.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Phoebe, we've had kind of a crazy relationship. We've broken up, gotten back together, broken up again...

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, but look at us now!

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: I know. And I want to spend the rest of my life with you. Will you marry me?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yes! Oh my God, yes!

jokes.text: Monica asks 'How's my girl?' and Amy says 'I'm fine' — Monica meant the baby
jokes.setup: Monica enters and greets the baby and Amy.
jokes.punchline: Amy interprets 'How's my girl?' as being directed at her and answers for herself.
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection gag — well-known template but Amy's self-centeredness makes it character-specific rather than generic. Functional.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, yes! Yes, I will marry you!

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: I love you so much.

dialogue.speaker: Random fan
dialogue.line: Oh, I'm so happy for you two! Congratulations!

jokes.text: Amy pierced Emma's ears — "Ta-da!"
jokes.setup: Amy presents Rachel with a gift for letting her stay.
jokes.punchline: The gift is pierced ears on Rachel's infant daughter — Amy is proud of this.
jokes.explanation: Great escalation of Amy's character. The gift being irreversible body modification on an infant — presented with 'Ta-da!' — is exactly the kind of boundary-obliterating gift Amy would give. The horror of the moment is the comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.line: I don't understand why parents don't want me to style their babies. I have a great eye for fashion!

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.line: I put little outfits on them, tiny hats, little sunglasses... and the parents just take it all off!

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.line: I think they're just jealous of my vision. Babies are basically tiny models, you know?

dialogue.speaker: Amy
dialogue.line: Plus, I only keep them for like eight hours at a time while I do the styling. That's not unreasonable!

jokes.text: "Doesn't it make her nose look smaller?"
jokes.setup: Everyone reacts in horror to Emma's pierced ears.
jokes.punchline: Amy's defense: it creates a flattering visual proportion for the baby's nose.
jokes.explanation: Superb character joke. Amy's concern about an infant's nose size in proportion to ear jewelry is simultaneously hilarious and a perfect revelation of her shallow value system. The delivery of this line as a genuine aesthetic defense is what makes it land. High quotability. Perfectly in character.

jokes.text: "If I had told you, then it wouldn't have been a surprise, now would it?"
jokes.setup: Rachel demands to know how Amy could pierce Emma's ears without telling her.
jokes.punchline: Amy's logic: she kept it secret because that's what makes a gift a surprise — standard surprise logic applied catastrophically.
jokes.explanation: Amy's logic is internally consistent and therefore funnier than pure stupidity would be. She's not wrong about surprise logic — she just failed to identify that this gift category requires consent. The calm reasoning is the comedy.

jokes.text: "I think she looks cute. But I am wrong."
jokes.setup: Everyone is horrified about Emma's pierced ears. Chandler breaks the tension.
jokes.punchline: Chandler admits he thinks she looks cute, then pre-emptively self-corrects — without anyone challenging him.
jokes.explanation: Classic Chandler beat. He voices a genuine opinion, reads the room instantly, and capitulates before anyone else responds. The self-correction without prompting is very Chandler and delivers an excellent laugh. High economy.

jokes.text: "Because there are so many terrible sights in this world. Like war. Or that thing in Joey's refrigerator. Remember? It was in a milk carton, but it looked like meat?"
jokes.setup: Ross presses Rachel on why she doesn't want Emma to see.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's escalating list of terrible sights: war, then 'that thing in Joey's refrigerator' — placing a domestic gross-out on the same moral plane as global conflict.
jokes.explanation: Good deflection escalation. The pivot from 'war' to 'Joey's refrigerator thing' is funny precisely because of the absurd equivalence. The specificity of 'milk carton but it looked like meat' paints a vivid enough picture to be gross and funny.

jokes.text: "Please tell me those are clip-ons!" / "Oh, they're real."
jokes.setup: Ross finally sees Emma's ears and reacts with horror.
jokes.punchline: His desperate hope that they're clip-ons is immediately dashed.
jokes.explanation: Functional reveal comedy. The clip-ons hope is a good specific detail — it shows Ross immediately searching for an escape hatch. Not particularly inventive but serves the scene.

jokes.text: "Hey! Monica can be cool and fun at organized indoor projects."
jokes.setup: Amy claims Rachel isn't a 'cool, fun aunt' in response to being called irresponsible. Monica objects.
jokes.punchline: Chandler defends Monica by limiting the domain of her coolness to 'organized indoor projects' — damning with faint praise.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Chandler line. He's defending Monica while simultaneously and accurately characterizing her limitations. 'Organized indoor projects' is hilariously specific and true. The fact that he means it as praise makes it funnier. Good character work for both Chandler and Monica.

jokes.text: "I am going to be a baby stylist."
jokes.setup: Rachel pushes Amy to think about her future. Amy says she's figured it out.
jokes.punchline: Amy's career revelation: baby stylist.
jokes.explanation: Perfect character payoff. Amy has absorbed exactly nothing from the piercing disaster — instead, she's converted it into a business plan. The fact that she's constructed a career path from an act of boundary violation is both horrifying and hilarious. 'Baby stylist' is a funny concept well-integrated with everything we've seen Amy do.

jokes.text: "That's not a thing!"
jokes.setup: Amy announces she will be a baby stylist.
jokes.punchline: Ross's flat, immediate, incredulous 'That's not a thing!'
jokes.explanation: Four words of absolute maximum economy delivering the audience's exact reaction. The bluntness is funnier than any elaborate rebuttal. This kind of reaction beat is a hallmark of well-tuned ensemble comedy.

jokes.text: "Well, it should be. I'm gonna help babies learn how to accessorize, what colors to wear, what clothes are slimming." / "Babies don't care if they're slim!" / "Enter Amy."
jokes.setup: Amy defends the baby stylist concept with her vision.
jokes.punchline: Rachel protests that babies don't care about being slim; Amy responds 'Enter Amy' — presenting herself as the solution to a problem that doesn't exist.
jokes.explanation: Amy's 'Enter Amy' is a brilliantly self-aggrandizing response to a non-problem she created. The escalation from 'babies don't care' to 'that's where Amy comes in' perfectly encapsulates her delusional entrepreneurial spirit.

jokes.text: Amy's response to Rachel's protest: 'Well, it should be.' Then: 'Enter Amy.'
jokes.setup: Rachel insists baby styling is not a real job. Babies don't care if they're slim.
jokes.punchline: 'Well, it should be' followed by 'Enter Amy' — she's positioning herself as the pioneer of an as-yet non-existent field.
jokes.explanation: 'Enter Amy' is a brilliantly theatrical self-introduction in the third person — delivered by Amy about herself. The structure of 'Well, it should be. Enter Amy.' is a perfect mini-escalation that also defines the character's grandiosity. Very quotable.

jokes.text: "No more falafel for you!" — Ross's empty threat to Amy
jokes.setup: Ross is furious at Amy but, mid-threat, realizes he has no leverage over her.
jokes.punchline: He defaults to the falafel vendor persona Amy assigned him — threatening to cut off her falafel supply as his only weapon.
jokes.explanation: Superb callback payoff. The falafel vendor running gag climaxes here with Ross — unable to find any other threat — weaponizing Amy's own delusion against her. It's funny, it's character-specific, it rewards the whole episode's setup, and 'No more falafel for you!' is a perfect Seinfeld-ian exclamation. One of the episode's highest-quality moments.

jokes.text: "If you don't hold it in, you don't get all the nutrients."
jokes.setup: Mike says he needs to go to the bathroom. Phoebe tells him to wait.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's reasoning: if you hold in urine, you absorb more nutrients from it — a completely invented physiological principle.
jokes.explanation: Quintessential Phoebe joke. She has invented a physiological myth and delivers it with complete confidence. The absurdism is grounded in character — Phoebe has always had an alternative understanding of science. The specific detail ('nutrients') is funnier than a vague claim would be.

jokes.text: "Get a load of this. She's proposing to him!" / "Guess we know who wears the pants in that family."
jokes.setup: Phoebe's proposal appears on the Jumbotron. A stranger in the crowd comments.
jokes.punchline: The stranger's sexist commentary is then challenged — and leads to Phoebe fighting back.
jokes.explanation: The 'pants in the family' comment is a dated joke that exists mainly to give Phoebe something to react against. It's not particularly funny on its own — it's functional setup for Phoebe's reaction. Below average for the episode.

jokes.text: "Well, that's not very enlightened." then leading the arena in booing the heckler
jokes.setup: A man in the crowd makes a sexist comment about Phoebe's proposal.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe doesn't get mad — she calmly labels it 'not very enlightened,' then successfully turns the arena crowd against the man with a 'Boo you!'
jokes.explanation: Good Phoebe character moment. 'Not very enlightened' is very her — calm, ideological, slightly condescending. Successfully rallying an arena crowd against a heckler is a funny visual escalation.

jokes.text: Phoebe fights back against the booing crowd at the arena
jokes.setup: The arena crowd starts booing Phoebe's proposal. Phoebe reacts.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe shouts 'Hey! Hey! Boo us? Boo you!' — turning the arena confrontation into a Phoebe-vs.-Madison Square Garden standoff.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe fighting back against an entire arena is very funny and in-character. The 'Boo us? Boo you!' reversal is punchy and exactly the right level of Phoebe defiance.

jokes.text: "No, my mommy and daddy aren't home right now."
jokes.setup: The adoption agency calls Joey about the letter. Joey conducts the call.
jokes.punchline: Joey maintains the fiction that he is a child, telling the caller his parents aren't home — cementing the agency's impression and completing the bit.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant callback execution. Rather than correct the agency's misimpression, Joey leans fully into the child persona — either because he doesn't want to correct them or because he genuinely thinks it's working. The 'mommy and daddy' detail is perfect. This is a great payoff to the entire letter subplot and arguably the second-best single line in the episode after 'Baby Kangaroo Tribbiani.'

jokes.text: Chandler announces 'Joey, get Amy's bags. She is moving out.' — the group cheers
jokes.setup: Chandler has had enough of Amy after the pierced ears incident.
jokes.punchline: The group's immediate, enthusiastic cheering at the news Amy is moving out functions as the punchline.
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom crowd-pleaser beat. Functional but relies on accumulated goodwill rather than its own craft. The cheering reaction carries most of the weight.

jokes.text: "Just us sisters back together again like when we were kids. Except without that stupid Jill. Oh. Who has gotten fat, by the way."
jokes.setup: Amy has a vulnerable moment about wanting sisterly bonding with Rachel.
jokes.punchline: She immediately adds that their other sister Jill — who she just remembered — has 'gotten fat.'
jokes.explanation: Funny because Amy's moment of genuine sentimentality is immediately polluted by her cattiness. The 'Oh' — her catching herself — before the revelation makes it funnier. Amy cannot sustain sincerity for more than two sentences.

jokes.text: "Oh, my God! I thought she was on Atkins." / "She was. Carbs found her."
jokes.setup: Rachel is shocked Jill gained weight given she was on Atkins.
jokes.punchline: Amy: 'Carbs found her.' — as if carbohydrates are a predator that tracked Jill down.
jokes.explanation: One of the best written lines in the episode. 'Carbs found her' is a three-word joke with brilliant personification — carbohydrates as a relentless hunter, Jill as prey. The economy is extraordinary. It's sharp, surprising, and immediately quotable. This is professional-grade comedy writing that holds up to any scrutiny.

jokes.text: Amy accidentally calls Emma 'Ella' at the reconciliation moment
jokes.setup: Amy and Rachel have just had a genuine bonding moment; Amy compliments Emma's pierced ears again
jokes.punchline: In the moment of warmth, Amy STILL calls the baby Ella — she simply cannot retain the correct name
jokes.explanation: A satisfying running gag payoff — Amy hasn't changed at all despite the apparent reconciliation. The fact that it comes at the warm resolution moment makes it funnier. Consistent callback.

jokes.text: "It's in the cake, isn't it?"
jokes.setup: Mike says Phoebe can promise to say yes 'however and whenever' he proposes, then she lists — basketball, skywriting, 'some lame guy who hides it in cake.'
jokes.punchline: Phoebe immediately clocks that the ring is in the current cake — she both revealed the method and guessed it instantly.
jokes.explanation: Good self-sabotage joke. Phoebe lists the methods to signal openness, inadvertently lands on the right one, and immediately figures it out. Her expression of 'Oh no' is implied in the script's structure. It's a funny pattern — she keeps accidentally ruining proposals.

jokes.text: "Where else would lame Mr. No Balls hide it?"
jokes.setup: Phoebe has just guessed that the ring is in the cake.
jokes.punchline: She doubles down — calling Mike 'lame Mr. No Balls' in the same breath as she's figured out his sweet proposal.
jokes.explanation: Callback to 'balls' language from earlier in the same scene, now deployed as an insult mid-romantic moment. Phoebe's horror at her own behavior is what makes this funny — she's genuinely trying but keeps destroying the moment.

jokes.text: Mike begins to propose formally, then Phoebe interrupts with 'Wait. Oh, wait.' — reacts to something (presumably checking the cake), then 'Oh, no.'
jokes.setup: Mike finally gives up on fancy proposals and decides to propose simply and sincerely. He begins.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe interrupts, apparently finds the ring in the cake, and says 'Oh, no' — she's ruined yet another attempt by being too alert.
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy inferred from context — Phoebe presumably digs into the cake looking for the ring. The escalation of Phoebe ruining proposals is consistent and builds toward the genuine moment.

jokes.text: "She's gonna be Mrs. No Balls!"
jokes.setup: Mike's proposal succeeds and Phoebe says yes. The crowd cheers.
jokes.punchline: The same heckler from earlier calls out 'She's gonna be Mrs. No Balls!' — apparently having stayed invested in the entire subplot.
jokes.explanation: Decent callback to close out the arena subplot. The heckler reappearing for a final comment is a satisfying button. 'Mrs. No Balls' as a surname is a good silly button. Not deeply crafted but it works as a capper.

jokes.text: "So how's the baby-styling business going?" / "Not that great. It's almost as if people don't want to hear that their babies are ugly." / "That's shocking."
jokes.setup: Tag scene: Amy has apparently launched her baby-styling career after the episode's events.
jokes.punchline: Amy's finding is that parents don't like being told their babies are ugly — delivered as a baffling discovery rather than an obvious truth. Joey's 'That's shocking' is the kicker.
jokes.explanation: Strong tag joke. Amy has launched the career and found the first obstacle to be parents' sensitivity about their babies' appearance. Her bafflement ('it's almost as if') at an obvious social truth is perfect Amy character comedy. Joey's dry 'That's shocking' — the rare case of Joey using deadpan sarcasm — is the ideal button.

jokes.text: Ross walks by ignoring Amy entirely after everything — "He's rude."
jokes.setup: Amy calls out to Ross twice. He passes by without acknowledging her.
jokes.punchline: Amy's verdict: 'He's rude.' — from someone who spent the episode not knowing who he was, refusing to recognize him, and calling him a falafel vendor.
jokes.explanation: Perfect episode-closing callback. After spending the entire episode failing to recognize or acknowledge Ross's identity, Amy has the audacity to call him rude for not responding to her. The irony is rich and well-earned. Ross's silent revenge — playing the falafel vendor card one last time by ignoring her — is a satisfying final note. Strong structural close.

tmdb_overview: To help her younger sister, Amy, become a more responsible person, Rachel overrides Ross' strong protests and allows Amy to baby-sit Emma but soon regrets that decision. Meanwhile, Joey volunteers to write a recommendation letter for Monica and Chandler's adoption agency, however, he's concerned about not sounding smart. Also, Phoebe unknowingly thwarts Mike's "anniversary" surprise for her.
insight: Sister dynamics drive Season 10's sharpest character comedy episode.
